item.title: Granite Switch 4.1 Unifies Chat, Decision‑Making and Speech on a Single Endpoint
item.description:
Granite Switch 4.1 Unifies Chat, Decision‑Making and Speech on a Single Endpoint

Granite Switch 4.1 introduces a family of models that pack chat, decision‑making and speech transcription capabilities into a single endpoint while using roughly the same GPU memory as the base model alone.

🔍 Overview

  • New model variants: Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑8B and Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑30B.
  • Each variant bundles three activated LoRA (aLoRA) adapters:
    • a Decision aLoRA for general‑purpose decision tasks (e.g., v1/systemone).
    • a Guardian aLoRA that, on average, outperforms Jev 1.13, Microsoft‑Decision‑1, GPT‑Luna‑Decisions and Clef‑Flash on safety‑related decision tasks.
    • Granite‑Speech‑5.0‑Turbo‑CTC, the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR Leaderboard, used for transcription.
  • The combined model occupies approximately the same VRAM as the underlying base model, delivering “more capabilities with fewer GPUs.”

🧩 How it works

  • The adapters are built as cache‑efficient Activated LoRAs. The KV cache generated by the base model during one generation can be reused for any subsequent adapter‑based request.
  • Recent vLLM contributions accelerate low‑rank adapter inference.
  • A co‑located ASR encoder enables the model to switch between chat, decision and spoken requests with “blazing fast speeds.”
  • An example Space – Speech‑to‑Decisions – shows granite-switch-4.1-8b transcribing audio, generating summaries, screening for harmful content and evaluating 15 user‑defined flags in real time on a single endpoint.

⚙️ Key details

Model Size Built‑in adapters
Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑8B 8 B parameters Decision aLoRA, Guardian aLoRA, Granite‑Speech‑5.0‑Turbo‑CTC
Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑30B 30 B parameters Decision aLoRA, Guardian aLoRA, Granite‑Speech‑5.0‑Turbo‑CTC
  • Performance: In a “race” against Jev‑27B (frozen Qwen base + 1 generic decision LoRA), Granite‑Switch‑4.1‑30B completed a real‑world, 5‑step RAG workflow faster.
  • Custom use case: A 3 B‑parameter Granite Switch model navigated the classic Doom game at 60–100 decisions / second, compared with Jev’s reported 10 decisions / second, and could also narrate and answer questions while playing.
  • Granite Libraries provide a repository of specialized adapters that can be mixed with the general‑purpose decision adapter at little extra cost because they share the base model’s KV cache.

🚀 Availability

  • The 8B and 30B models are released with “batteries included”, i.e., pre‑compiled with a helpful set of adapters.
  • Users may compose their own Granite Switch models by mixing adapters from Granite Libraries.
  • An Adapter SDK for training adapters in Mellea, along with tutorials and support, is planned for future release.

💡 Why it matters

  • Consolidates three major AI functionalities—chat, decision‑making and speech—into one model, simplifying deployment and reducing hardware requirements.
  • Cache‑efficient design and vLLM acceleration make multi‑modal switching real‑time, opening possibilities for interactive applications such as live transcription with instant safety screening.
  • The open‑adapter ecosystem encourages community extensions and custom task specialization without large memory overhead.

#GraniteSwitch #AIAdapters #SpeechRecognition #DecisionModels

Source: Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint

item.title: Serving llama.cpp Decision Models on SageMaker with Text and Structured Paths
item.description:
Serving llama.cpp Decision Models on SageMaker with Text and Structured Paths

Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure.

🔍 Overview

  • Two deployment paths are available from the same packaged model (Figure 1).
  • Text‑generation path uses the AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI‑compatible chat completions API.
  • Structured‑decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options.

🧩 How it Works

Standard text‑generation path

  1. Package the model as model.tar.gz in Amazon S3.
  2. Reference the published AWS DLC image for llama.cpp directly.
  3. At container start, the DLC scans /opt/ml/model for the first .gguf file.
  4. The container maps POST /invocations to llama‑server at /v1/chat/completions.
  5. SM_LLAMA_CPP_* environment variables are passed as arguments to llama.cpp.

Structured‑decision path (SemIf)

  1. Use AWS CodeBuild to build a child image that keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries.
  2. Replace the default entry point with a SageMaker‑compatible SemIf adapter.
  3. Store the child image in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR).
  4. The adapter reads the final‑position logits and state that the llama‑server API does not expose, and returns a decision schema with option_ids, probabilities, option_logits, plus prompt, timing, and model metadata.

⚙️ Key Details

  • The AWS DLC for llama.cpp accepts the OpenAI Chat Completions schema.
  • Generated text is found in choices[0].message.content of the response.
  • SemIf uses a constrained decision schema (no chat messages) and returns:
    • option_ids
    • probabilities
    • raw option_logits
    • prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata.
  • Stable option IDs let applications apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing free‑form text.
  • SemIf belongs to a broader class of decision models that score application‑defined outcomes from unstructured state. Other implementations mentioned are Jev, TypeSafe’s decision model, Kev, and Strands Decider 2B.

🚀 When to Use Which Path

  • Standard text‑generation – Use when you need OpenAI‑compatible chat completions via InvokeEndpoint.
  • Structured‑decision (SemIf) – Build a child image only when you need direct access to logits or state, such as:
    • Routing a case to a specific queue
    • Extracting a single value from a known set
    • Assigning incident priority
    • Checking a policy outcome
    • Selecting an agent action
  • Keep authorization and deterministic business rules outside the model and validate probabilities before treating them as operational confidence.

💡 Why It Matters

  • The managed SageMaker AI path removes the need to run custom inference servers for quantized llama.cpp models.
  • By swapping in a SemIf adapter, the same model can serve both free‑form text and structured decision outputs, reducing model duplication.
  • Applications gain deterministic, audit‑ready probabilities while still leveraging a single underlying LLM.

#SageMaker #llama.cpp #SemIf #AIInference #DecisionModels

Source: Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Open-weight d1‑3B and d1‑omni‑600M decision models released with multimodal fast inference
item.description:
Open-weight d1‑3B and d1‑omni‑600M decision models released with multimodal fast inference

A new family of open‑weight decision models, d1‑3B and d1‑omni‑600M, is now available on Hugging Face. They are built on Liquid Foundation Models and are designed for fast, structured decisions with multimodal inputs.

🔍 Overview

  • d1‑3B scores 48.57 on Decision Index 0.2.1, the highest among models under 10 B parameters.
  • d1‑omni‑600M, an early research release, supports text + image or text + audio inputs.
  • Both models are open‑weight and can be downloaded from Hugging Face.

🧩 How it works

  • Backbones
    • d1‑3B is trained from LFM2.5‑VL‑3B, a decoder‑only visual‑language model.
    • d1‑omni‑600M is trained from LFM2.5‑Encoder‑350M, a bidirectional encoder that adds vision and audio encoders.
  • Decision‑only architecture – unlike generative models, these models answer in a single forward pass and do not produce tokens.
  • Multimodal support
    • d1‑3B: text + image.
    • d1‑omni‑600M: text + image or text + audio.

⚙️ Key details

Model Parameters (≈) Input modalities Backbone Notable strength
d1‑3B 3 B Text, Image LFM2.5‑VL‑3B (decoder‑only) Highest decision quality under 10 B; edge inference < 50 ms
d1‑omni‑600M 600 M Text + Image or Text + Audio LFM2.5‑Encoder‑350M (bidirectional) Good performance with a quarter of the parameters of a 2 B baseline
  • Benchmark performance
    • d1‑3B achieves a mean score of 82.9, the highest in the benchmark table and above Decider 4B.
    • d1‑omni‑600M scores 78.4, surpassing Decider 2B (77.1) with only a quarter of the parameters.
    • Benchmarked on seven public datasets covering reading comprehension, toxicity detection, intent classification, medical QA, and cross‑lingual understanding.
  • Speed
    • Edge inference (NVIDIA Jetson): 16 ms (AGX Thor), 26 ms (AGX Orin), 50 ms (Orin Nano) per question; under 50 ms on all measured devices.
    • Three questions take only 1.3× the time of one (AGX Thor: 16 ms → 20 ms).
    • GPU inference (GeForce RTX 4090, Jetson AGX Orin): under 10 ms per question; 384 px image processed in under 18 ms.
    • No speed numbers reported for d1‑omni‑600M in this release.
  • Vision capability of d1‑3B validated on standard vision benchmarks; d1‑omni‑600M handles all three modalities, though private vision and audio decision benchmarks are not reported.

🚀 Availability

  • Both models are open‑weight and can be downloaded from Hugging Face:
    • d1‑3B
    • d1‑omni‑600M
  • Demo space: System One Arcade on Hugging Face.
  • d1‑omni‑600M model card provides usage instructions.

💡 Why it matters

  • d1‑3B delivers the highest decision quality for its size, making it suitable when accuracy is paramount.
  • d1‑omni‑600M offers strong performance with a small footprint, ideal for resource‑constrained environments.
  • Fast single‑pass inference enables real‑time structured decision making on edge devices.

#DecisionModels #MultimodalAI #EdgeInference #OpenSource

Source: Multimodal open d1 decision models for the edge

item.title: Cloudflare and Strands Release Open Decision Models for AI Agents
item.description:
Cloudflare and Strands Release Open Decision Models for AI Agents

Cloudflare and Strands Labs released open-source decision models and RL fine-tuning tools designed to help AI agents make fast, structured choices efficiently.

🔍 Overview

Two new open-source “decision” models were released this week, along with supporting services, aimed at replacing expensive, general-purpose LLM calls for routine agent tasks. Cloudflare shipped Clef and Clef‑flash, and Strands Labs published Strands Decider 2B.

🧩 How it works

Decision models are optimized to return structured choices (not freeform text), such as routing a ticket, deciding to escalate, or approving/denying an action. They operate with lower latency and cost than calling a full LLM, making them useful for agent routing, guardrails, and tool selection.

⚙️ Key details

  • Clef and Clef‑flash (Cloudflare): Open-source models with Apache‑2.0 license. Cloudflare added an RL fine‑tuning service for them on Workers AI.
  • Strands Decider 2B (Strands Labs): A 2‑billion parameter open-source model with weights and training scripts published, designed to run locally and return confidence‑scored choices in tens to low hundreds of milliseconds.

💡 Why it matters

  • Decision models let agents make cheap, fast, and calibrated choices with lower latency and cost than calling a full LLM.
  • Small, calibrated decision models make it practical to offload routine, high‑volume decisions from expensive LLM calls — lowering cost and making agent tool calls safer by verifying arguments or gating premature actions.
  • Clef’s Apache‑2.0 weights and Worker hosting affect on‑prem versus cloud tradeoffs.
  • For teams building agents, moving routine classification or tool‑selection logic to a decision model can cut latency and infer costs.

#Cloudflare #StrandsLabs #DecisionModels #AIAgents #OpenSource #RLAIF

item.title: New LLM plugin adds support for TypeSafe AI's Jev decision model
item.description:
New LLM plugin adds support for TypeSafe AI’s Jev decision model

A new plugin has been released for LLM to provide support for the Jev model from TypeSafe AI. This development, announced on 22nd September 2026, allows users to integrate Jev into their existing LLM workflows for specific decision-making tasks.

⚙️ Key details

Users can install the plugin via the command line using llm install llm-typesafe. After installation, users must set an API key using the command llm keys set typesafe.

🧩 How it works

The Jev model is categorized as a “System One” or “Decision Model.” It supports three primary types of query processing:

Answer Type Function
noul Performs yes/no questioning and scoring
choice Classifies input into specific categories provided via criteria
score Evaluates input based on a ranked list of criteria

🚀 Availability

The plugin is currently available for installation. Users interested in utilizing the Jev model should note that there is a waitlist for API access.

#LLM #Jev #TypeSafe #DecisionModels

Source: Release: llm-typesafe 0.1a0
